lede: The book opens in a wizard's workroom under a dim red sun. Turjan of Miir is trying to grow life in vats, but he only gets pitiful, misshapen creatures. A sage tells him that the all-knowing Pandelume lives in the far land of Embelyon. Pandelume agrees to teach him, but first Turjan must steal an amulet from Prince Kandive the Golden in the city of Kaiin.

points.body: The sun is old and could go out at any time. Ancient science has shrunk to a few spells: *a thousand spells were known to sorcery* once, and only a fraction survive. People know the end is coming and live with an elegant, tired indifference.

Turjan packs his mind with *the Excellent Prismatic Spray, Phandaal's Mantle of Stealth, and the Spell of the Slow Hour*. A spell is learned by heart and disappears once it is cast. Dungeons & Dragons borrowed this rule, and it is still called “Vancian magic.”
Pandelume must never be seen, and everything has its price. He *drives a hard bargain*, so Turjan's first lesson is a theft at Kandive's festival in Kaiin.

expressions.zh: An idiom meaning to insist on terms that favor you. It sums up Pandelume's character.
A fatalistic remark that sets the tone of the whole book.
Kaiin is in the middle of a celebration, which gives Turjan cover for the theft.

questions: Why do you think Vance made magic a matter of memory rather than inborn power?
What does the decayed, festive city of Kaiin tell you about this world?

lede: Turjan brings back the amulet, helps Pandelume subdue a screaming monster with his eyes shut, and becomes his apprentice. He learns the abstract art Pandelume calls “mathematics,” the secret of renewed youth, and at last how to make living beings. The wild dark-haired woman who attacked him is T'sais, a flawed creation of Pandelume's. Turjan makes a perfect sister for her, T'sain.

points.body: For Vance, mathematics is the deepest magic of all. It is the abstract structure behind every spell, and it is what lets Turjan finally create life.
She was made *with a flaw in the synthesis*: she sees beauty as ugliness and everything good as hateful, so she strikes out at the world.
T'sain has the same pattern without the flaw. When the two meet, T'sais finally has someone to talk to, and she decides to go to Earth to look for what she cannot find in Embelyon.

expressions.en: with a flaw in the synthesis
expressions.zh: Synthesis means making something from parts. The flaw is in how she was put together, not in her will.
One of the things Turjan learns. In this world, wizards can live for a very long time.
T'sais's first impulse when T'sain embraces her. A deeper feeling rises against it.

questions: Is T'sais responsible for her hatred? How does Vance want us to see her?
What does it mean that knowledge in this book is called “mathematics”?

lede: The second story switches viewpoint. The wizard Mazirian walks through his garden of strange plants: talking flowers, blossoms that pulse like sea anemones, red-mouthed shrubs that eat mice. He is obsessed with a woman who rides a black horse past his garden at dusk, and he wants to capture her. Halfway through, we learn that the thumb-sized prisoner in his cellar is Turjan.

points.body: The garden is beautiful and monstrous at once, much like Mazirian himself.
Mazirian has shrunk Turjan and keeps him in a little maze with a dragon, to force the secret of creating life out of him. Turjan's eyes stay *as vacant as those of a lizard*.
Before he sets out, Mazirian *forced five spells upon his brain*. Holding that many takes great effort, and each one he uses is gone.

expressions.en: as vacant as those of a lizard
expressions.zh: A simile for an empty, unreadable stare.

expressions.en: forced five spells upon his brain
expressions.zh: Shows how much strain Vancian magic puts on the mind.
Enchanted boots that carry Mazirian at speed. Vance likes plain names for magical things.

questions: How does the garden reflect Mazirian's personality?
How did your view of the story change when you learned who the prisoner was?

lede: Mazirian chases the woman into the forest of fable, spending his spells as he goes. He buys news from a Twk-man on a dragonfly, spins a man-eating Deodand to pieces, splits the ghoul Thrang with the Prismatic Spray, and dives to a ruined temple at the bottom of a lake. She escapes every time, and finally leads him between blood-sucking grass and whipping black trees. She is T'sain, and she has given her life to free Turjan.

points.body: The Twk-men trade news for salt, the Deodand is a handsome eater of men, Thrang is a ghoul. The forest works like a catalogue of the dying world's creatures.
Every spell Mazirian uses leaves him weaker. Vance turns the chase into a slow countdown.
Turjan grieves over her: *more noble are you than I, who used the only life you knew for my freedom.* Then he takes her body to the vats to make her again. His tenderness has a chill in it.

expressions.zh: The name of the woods. It suggests that the old stories have come true here.
To cut away one's own power. Each spell Mazirian casts does exactly that.
Turjan's name for T'sain. She is his creation, and also the one he loves.

questions: Is Turjan a hero, a victim, or something else in this story?
What does T'sain's sacrifice say about created beings and the people who make them?

lede: T'sais keeps her promise and goes back to Pandelume to ask to be sent to Earth. He cannot change her eyes, but he gives her a rune that turns back hostile magic and a pouch of jewels. She lands near a mossy ruined castle. The first human scene she sees is Liane the Wayfarer torturing a peasant couple by a fire.

points.body: He warns her that *terrible things rove the dark* on Earth, and the story soon proves him right.
Liane, who struts *like a plumed cock*, is the hero of the fourth story. Here we see him first as a torturer.
T'sais draws her sword for the first time, *mindful of Pandelume's warnings*. Her hatred of the world finally has a real target.

expressions.zh: A rooster with fine feathers, an image of strutting vanity.
How T'sais thinks of humans after what she sees.
Mindful means keeping something in mind. She is careful, not reckless.

questions: T'sais can only see ugliness. Does the first scene on Earth prove her right?
Why do you think Vance introduces Liane through T'sais's eyes?

lede: T'sais crosses the endless Modavna Moor. A gang of bandits wants her jewels, drags her into a stone hut and draws lots to decide who will have her first. They fight over cheating at the lots, and her sword flies up to join the brawl. After she escapes, a Deodand hunts her across the moor. She stumbles into a cottage and wakes to find a man in a black hood feeding her soup. His name is Etarr.

points.body: This is the darkest part of the book. Vance describes the threat plainly but moves quickly past it.

points.h: The cottage and a lesson in beauty
points.body: T'sais admits *I know not what love is*. Etarr starts to show her that some things in the world are beautiful.
He is *Etarr the Masked*: the witch Javanne cursed his face, and he hides it out of shame. Two damaged people begin to help each other.

expressions.en: I know not what love is
expressions.zh: Old-fashioned word order for “I don't know what love is.” Vance's style is full of this archaic syntax.
An epithet, like those of the heroes in old epics.

expressions.en: Surely one's life was one's own
expressions.zh: T'sais's thought, a quiet claim of independence.

questions: How does Etarr's damage mirror T'sais's?
What does Etarr teach T'sais, and what does she give him in return?

lede: Etarr goes to the witches' Black Sabbath to find Javanne, and T'sais insists on coming. At the height of the revels, the green legions of Valdaran the Just descend from the sky blowing horns. Etarr catches the fleeing Javanne. She casts a spell to rob him of his will, but T'sais's rune turns it back on her. The three of them fly to an ancient god to receive the justice each deserves.

points.body: The witches' gathering is the most grotesque set piece in the book, and Vance describes it lavishly.
The rune Pandelume gave T'sais finally matters. Javanne's own magic defeats her.

The god will *give each his due*: *To each who comes, justice is done*. Javanne's beauty is stripped away and Etarr is freed from her curse. Even at the Sabbath, Etarr whispers, *Even here is beauty*.

expressions.zh: Due means what someone is owed. This is the old idea of justice as giving each person what they deserve.
Etarr's lesson for T'sais: beauty can be found even in the grotesque.
A spell that is remarkably short. Vance is dryly funny about magic.

questions: Is the god's justice satisfying, or does it unsettle you?
How has T'sais changed since the start of her story?

lede: Healed from his wounds, Liane walks through the forest singing. That morning he killed a spice merchant, and while burying the body he dug up a copper ring carved with runes: when he slips it over his head, he steps into a hidden space where no one can see him. A Twk-man tells him a beautiful golden witch, Lith, has come to Thamber Meadow. Liane tries to seduce her, and she throws mud in his face. She says that if he brings back the other half of her golden tapestry from Chun the Unavoidable, she will be his.

points.body: Liane is vain, charming and casually murderous. Small things *conspired to exasperate him*, but he never doubts himself.
Liane believes that *every unpleasantness carried with it compensation*. That optimism is about to be tested.
Lith shows him a tapestry of a lost valley, her home Ariventa. The missing half is held by *Chun the Unavoidable*.

expressions.zh: Exasperate means to annoy greatly. The pompous phrasing mocks Liane's self-importance.

expressions.en: every unpleasantness carried with it compensation
expressions.zh: Liane's comfortable philosophy, that every bad thing comes with a reward.
The name itself is a warning.

questions: Do you find Liane likable? Why or why not?
What clues does Vance give that Lith's offer is dangerous?

lede: Liane arrives in Kaiin, trades magic tricks with wizards at an inn and asks about Chun, but no one will talk. The next day, in the ruins of the old city, an old man shows him bodies lying *like crushed flies*. Liane kills the old man with a block of granite. He finds the marble hall where half the tapestry hangs, and something on the wall moves. The final scene returns to Lith's cottage.

points.body: The city's beauty is full of decay, just like the world.

points.h: A man who will not listen
points.body: The old man's warning is clear, and Liane ignores it. Vanity is his fatal flaw.
*I am Chun the Unavoidable.* Chun brings Lith two golden threads, and we finally understand what her tapestry is made of. It is one of the great twist endings in fantasy.

expressions.zh: A vivid simile for Chun's victims.

expressions.en: like an old man creeping to his death-bed
expressions.zh: How Liane moves near the end. His swagger is gone.

expressions.en: a robe of eyeballs threaded on silk
expressions.zh: Chun's garment, a horrifying image that explains the whole story.

questions: Who is the real villain of this story: Liane, Chun, or Lith?
Why does Vance end the story in Lith's cottage rather than in the marble hall?

lede: Prince Kandive the Golden sends his nephew Ulan Dhor to the lost city of Ampridatvir to retrieve two transparent metal tablets left by the last great sorcerer, Rogol Domedonfors. They are said to hold all the knowledge of the ancients. Ulan Dhor crosses the Melantine Gulf, follows two green-clad fishermen into the city, and rescues a girl in gray, Elai, from a man-eating Gaun.

points.body: An old letter about the city laments the decline of its people: *a surfeit of ease guts a man of strength.* The letter blames too much comfort for the city's decline.
Ampridatvir is full of machines with *ageless substance, eternal energies*. It is the clearest sign of how much humanity has lost.
The fishermen say the city is *ridden with ghosts*. Ulan Dhor soon finds stranger things than ghosts.

expressions.en: a surfeit of ease guts a man of strength
expressions.zh: A surfeit is too much of something. Too much comfort hollows a man out.
Full of ghosts. Ridden suggests infestation.
A description of the old machines that never stopped running.

questions: What does Ampridatvir suggest about the fate of advanced civilizations?
Why might Kandive really be sending Ulan Dhor so far away?

lede: Ulan Dhor discovers Ampridatvir's strangest secret: the people in green and the people in gray truly cannot see each other. They shop and play in the same square while acting as if the others do not exist. He and Elai fly an ancient air-car into the two temples, take both tablets and put together a message: go to the Tower of Destiny. Under a yellow dome, a brain that has slept for five thousand years wakes up.

points.body: *No one in Ampridatvir wears green*, Elai insists. The two sects ignore each other *by not so much as a glance*. It is Vance's sharpest satire of sectarian hatred.
The tablets lead to the Tower of Destiny, where a face forms in black metal and says cheerfully, *Greetings across time*.

Rogol Domedonfors is shocked to learn he has slept *over five thousand years*. Seeing his people still divided, he sets out to punish them, and Ulan Dhor and Elai escape. The last line is *Elai, you will like Kaiin.*

expressions.en: by not so much as a glance
expressions.zh: Not even one look. A precise description of deliberate blindness.
The first words of the waking mind, cheerful and eerie at once.
To contrive is to find a clever way. Ulan Dhor has no magic to bring home, but he is already planning how to satisfy Kandive.

questions: What real-world divisions does the green/gray blindness remind you of?
Is Rogol Domedonfors a savior or a tyrant?

lede: The last story is the longest and the most philosophical. Guyal of Sfere was born with *a void which ached for nourishment*, a hunger to know everything: what lies beyond the sky, where people come from. His father can only tell him that the Curator, guardian of the legendary Museum of Man, can answer such questions. Guyal sets off with his father's white horse, a magic egg-shaped tent, a glowing dagger and other gifts.

points.body: Guyal *had been born one apart from his fellows*. In a world that has given up, curiosity is a kind of rebellion.
*my fine white horse, my Expansible Egg for your shelter, my Scintillant Dagger*. These are fairy-tale gifts with science-fiction names.
On his way, Guyal meets strangers whose customs he does not understand. The dying Earth is full of small, closed worlds.

expressions.en: a void which ached for nourishment
expressions.zh: An emptiness that hurts to be filled. A strong metaphor for curiosity.
A portable shelter that expands. Vance's inventions are playful and precise.
Scintillant means sparkling. The dagger's light will matter later.

questions: Why is curiosity treated as a problem in Guyal's home?
How is Guyal's quest different from Turjan's or Liane's?

lede: Darkness rises *like ink in a basin*. Guyal sees lights in a valley town, and a girl in yellow invites him in while her uncle Ludowik plays the pipes without stopping. Guyal gets drunk and plays wild music; the girl dances, falls and foams at the mouth. He flees, and at dawn he looks back to see that the town is only a ruin. Past a mountain pass, he reaches Saponce, the town of the Saponids.

points.body: A ghost town that comes alive at night. Guyal does not know what is real.
Guyal describes a white figure floating high over the pass, and a Saponid calls it *a signal of woe*.
The Saponids call themselves *a highly civilized people*. Guyal soon learns how dangerous their manners can be.

expressions.zh: A simile for darkness spreading through the valley.
Woe is deep sorrow. An old-fashioned, poetic word.
The Saponids' proud description of themselves, which Vance uses ironically.

questions: What makes the night in Carchasel so unsettling?
What do you expect from people who insist they are highly civilized?

lede: Guyal has broken a Saponid law, and the town's leader says the penalty is light because it was only an oversight. Guyal must swear not to do it again, choose the most beautiful maiden in a pageant, and then escort her to the Museum of Man three leagues north. The girls all make themselves dirty and ugly on purpose. Guyal picks Shierl, the leader's daughter. In tears, she walks with him to the Museum, where a wailing voice calls them forward.

points.body: The penalty sounds mild, but it hides a yearly sacrifice. The Saponids accept it with *So it is; so it has been; so it will be*.
The town treats the pageant as an honor, but every girl knows what it means.
Guyal will not be a *cringing victim*. He faces *the ooze of terror, the sweat of horror* and goes in anyway.

expressions.en: So it is; so it has been; so it will be
expressions.zh: A ritual phrase of resignation. The Saponids have stopped asking why.
To cringe is to shrink back in fear.

expressions.en: the ooze of terror, the sweat of horror
expressions.zh: Parallel phrases that make fear feel physical.

questions: What do the Saponids' customs say about societies that ritualize fear?
Why does Guyal choose Shierl, and why does he go on?

lede: Deep in the Museum, a huge gray face is pressing through a hole in the wall. It is Blikdak, ruler of the demon world Jeldred, who wants to swallow all the knowledge in the Museum and is only waiting for the Curator to die. The Curator, Kerlin, is so old he is mad and believes he still lives in the vanished city of Thorsingol. Guyal and Shierl trick him into his own Chair of Clarity; his mind clears, and together the three find a way to destroy Blikdak.

points.body: Blikdak is born *from the mind of man*: a creature of human fear and hatred, the perfect enemy for a seeker of knowledge.

points.h: The mad Curator and the Chair of Clarity
points.body: *There is no Thorsingol*, Guyal has to tell him. The old man is lost in a past that is gone.
Guyal says *Knowledge is ours, Shierl—all of knowing to our call. And what shall we do?* The book ends with an open question rather than a triumph.

expressions.zh: A gentle but firm correction that brings the Curator back to the present.
Blikdak's origin: evil made by people themselves.

expressions.en: all of knowing to our call
expressions.zh: At our command. Guyal and Shierl now have every answer, but they still need a purpose.

questions: Why does the book end with a question instead of a victory?
After all six stories, what do you think gives life meaning on a dying Earth?
